issues.legal_issue: A court exercising review jurisdiction cannot delete an evidence-based finding merely because it considers the finding erroneous or because no formal issue was framed on the subject.
material_facts: The High Court had made observations about possession after considering the plaintiff’s and his witness’s evidence and other material on record, including the defendants’ application seeking an order requiring the plaintiff to vacate.
The defendants sought review of those observations principally on the ground that possession had not been framed as an issue or considered for decision.
The review application did not establish a qualifying ground such as new and important material or an error apparent on the face of the record.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its review jurisdiction by deleting the observations on possession; its review order was set aside and the observations were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 114 read with Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, review is confined to the specified grounds, including discovery of new and important matter despite due diligence, an error apparent on the face of the record, or an analogous sufficient reason. Review is not an appeal in disguise and cannot be used to rehear or correct a decision on its merits. An apparent error must be self-evident, not one requiring an extended process of reasoning. The Court relied on Haridas Das v. Usha Rani Banik, Meera Bhanja v. Nirmala Kumari Choudhury, Aribam Tuleshwar Sharma v. Aribam Pishak Sharma, Parsion Devi v. Sumitri Devi, Lily Thomas v. Union of India, Inderchand Jain v. Motilal, and State of West Bengal v. Kamal Sengupta.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party asked a court to reconsider and alter its earlier decision.
predicates.finding_based_on_record_evidence: The court made the challenged finding after considering evidence and other material in the record.
predicates.review_sought_to_remove_finding_without_: The review applicant sought removal of the finding without establishing new and important material, a self-evident error, or an analogous sufficient reason.

issues.definition: When a review applicant seeks to remove a finding made on the record without establishing a qualifying ground, the reviewing court cannot revisit the merits to alter it.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to frame a formal issue does not invalidate a finding on a matter that was pleaded, contested, and addressed through evidence when the parties understood the rival cases and suffered no prejudice.
material_facts: The pleadings of both sides contained averments about possession.

The plaintiff and a witness gave evidence supporting the plaintiff’s possession, and the defendants did not cross-examine the plaintiff on that point or lead evidence to establish their own possession.
The parties understood the competing positions on possession, and the omission of a separately framed issue caused no prejudice.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a separately framed issue on possession did not invalidate the finding or justify deleting it on review.
issues.legal_principle: A formal issue’s omission fades into insignificance when the parties understood the rival cases and extensive evidence was recorded without demur, provided the omission caused no prejudice. The Court applied Sri Gangai Vinayagar Temple v. Meenakshi Ammal.

rule.if: civil_case and matter_pleaded_by_parties and evidence_recorded_on_matter and parties_understood_rival_cases and no_prejudice_from_omission

predicates.civil_case: The matter was decided in a civil proceeding.
predicates.matter_pleaded_by_parties: The parties included the matter in their pleadings.
predicates.evidence_recorded_on_matter: The parties presented evidence addressing the matter.
predicates.parties_understood_rival_cases: The parties knew and contested each other’s positions on the matter.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_omission: The omission of a separately framed issue did not prejudice either party or vitiate the proceedings.

issues.definition: When a matter is pleaded and addressed by evidence, the parties understand their competing positions, and the missing formal issue causes no prejudice, that omission does not invalidate the finding.
